h1: AI consulting that ends in working systems
intro: 22 Signals offers AI consulting for established companies that know AI matters but have not turned it into results. We review how the business runs, find the processes worth automating or augmenting, rank them by value and effort, choose the tools, set the rules for safe use, and ship a working pilot your team actually uses.

sections.h: Why AI projects stall after the demo
p: Most companies have already tried something. A few people use ChatGPT or Copilot on their own, a vendor ran an impressive demo, and someone built a prototype over a weekend. Six months later nothing has changed in how the business runs.

The reasons are usually the same. Nobody picked the use case by value, so the first project was the most exciting one rather than the most useful. The data it needed was spread across inboxes and spreadsheets. Legal or compliance raised questions late. And the person who built the prototype went back to their day job, so it was never made reliable enough to depend on.
Good AI consulting fixes the order of work: decide what is worth doing, check the business is ready for it, agree the rules, then build something small that proves the value.

sections.h: The readiness review and how we rank use cases
p: The readiness review looks at four things. Data: where it lives, who owns it and whether it is clean enough for the first use cases. Systems: what your CRM, finance, document and communication tools can connect to. People: who will use AI daily and who will own it. Risk: client confidentiality, regulated data and contractual limits.

We then list every candidate use case and score it. Value covers hours saved each month, revenue at stake, cost of errors today and how often the task runs. Effort covers data availability, integration work, change for the team and risk. The result is a ranked list you can defend to a board, with quick wins at the top and bigger bets scheduled behind them.

An AI policy does not need to be long. It needs to say which tools are approved, which data can go into them, which outputs need a human review before they reach a client, and who to ask when something is unclear. We write it with your team and check vendor terms, including whether a provider can train on your data and where it is stored.

We align the rules with the frameworks your buyers and regulators already reference: the NIST AI Risk Management Framework in the US, the EU AI Act if you sell into Europe, ISO/IEC 42001 for companies that want a formal AI management system, and the privacy law you already follow, such as HIPAA for US healthcare data or GDPR and UK GDPR for personal data.

sections.h: Build or buy: choosing tools and vendors
p: Many use cases are already solved by tools you pay for. Microsoft 365 Copilot, Gemini in Google Workspace, ChatGPT Enterprise and Claude Team each fit different companies, and many industry tools now ship AI features. Buying is often the right first move.

Custom work makes sense when the process is specific to you, when the data cannot leave your systems, or when several tools need to work as one. In those cases we build on the major model providers through their APIs and keep the design portable, so you are not locked to one vendor if prices or quality change.

faqs.q: What does an AI consultant do?
faqs.a: An AI consultant finds where AI can save time, cut cost or create revenue in a business, plans how to adopt it safely, and helps put it in place. At 22 Signals, AI consulting includes a readiness review, ranked use cases, a roadmap, tool selection, governance rules and pilot builds, and the same team that advises also builds.

faqs.q: Where should a company start with AI?
faqs.a: Start with one process your team repeats every day that runs on documents, email or structured data, such as intake, reporting or follow-up. It should matter enough that saved hours are visible, but not be so risky that an error hurts a client. A focused pilot there proves value quickly and shows what the next step should be.

faqs.q: Do we need clean data before using AI?
faqs.a: Not perfect data, but usable data for the first use cases. Many good starting points, such as drafting, summarizing and triage, need very little preparation. Part of the readiness review is checking what you have and fixing only the gaps that block the first projects, rather than starting a long data program before anything ships.

faqs.q: How long does an AI consulting engagement take?
faqs.a: A readiness review and roadmap for one business unit take 5 to 7 days, and a first pilot typically ships 3 to 4 times faster than the usual market timeline. Larger companies with several departments, regulated data or vendor reviews take longer. We agree every date in writing before we start, and you see working output well before the full roadmap is complete.

faqs.q: Is it safe to put company data into AI tools?
faqs.a: It can be, with the right tools and rules. Business plans from the major providers let you keep your data out of model training, and many offer data residency options. We check vendor terms, set which data is allowed where, add human review for client-facing outputs, and write it all into a short policy your team can follow.

faqs.q: Should we build custom AI or buy existing tools?
faqs.a: Buy when an existing tool solves the problem well, which is common for drafting, meeting notes and general research. Build when the process is specific to you, when data must stay in your systems, or when several tools need to work together. Our recommendation for each use case comes with the reasoning, so you can judge it yourself.

faqs.q: How much does AI consulting cost?
faqs.a: It depends on scope: how many processes we review, whether you need a governance framework, how many pilots we build and how ready your data is. We don't publish prices. After a short call we send a written scope with dates, so you know what is included before committing to anything.
